entries.title: Commanders' Terry McLaurin Gets Carted Off After a Leg Injury
entries.summary: The veteran wide receiver injured his left leg in the first quarter of Monday's game.
entries.content:
Commanders wide receiver Terry McLaurin was carted off the field after suffering a lower leg injury in the first quarter of Monday's game against the 49ers.

With Washington trailing 13-3, McLaurin appeared to get his feet tangled with San Francisco corner Deommodore Lenoir on a third-down route. McLaurin reached for his left leg as he fell to the ground. He stayed down for some time as trainers put an air cast on his left leg. Teammates looked on as he was carted off to the locker room. Shortly after, the Commanders ruled him out for the rest of Monday's game.

https://x.com/TSN_Sports/status/2112346540794601655?s=20
The veteran wideout was in his second game back after missing Week 4 with a hamstring injury. Entering Monday, he had 14 catches for 203 yards and a touchdown this season.

entries.title: Judge Rules That North Carolina’s Mail-In Ballot Restrictions Will Remain Through the Midterms
entries.summary: The state’s election board made it easier to reject completed ballots in an eleventh-hour change last month.
entries.content:
A federal judge ruled Wednesday that North Carolina’s rigid new mail-in ballot policies will remain in place for the midterms, upholding a last-minute rule change that could make it easier for state officials to invalidate thousands of votes in November.

U.S. District Judge Thomas Schroeder, a George W. Bush appointee, said that it was already too late to overturn the policies, which the state's Republican-led board of elections passed hours before voters received their ballots in early September.

“Neither of the two Challenged Provisions, which are clearly stated on the absentee ballot materials — that the voter sign his or her own name and place their ballot in a sealed envelope provided by the county board of election — is burdensome, much less unduly so,” Schroeder wrote.

The judge said in his ruling that the plaintiffs — a coalition of civil rights groups — waited too long to move for an injunction, filing the request the day before officials began counting absentee ballots.

“We’re in the midst of election season,” Schroeder said at a hearing last week.  

The decision upholds some of the strictest vote-by-mail procedures in the country on North Carolina voters, who were the first in the country this cycle to receive their ballots. Schroeder’s ruling also comes as national efforts to curb or question mail-in voting intensify before Nov. 3.

The new guidelines make it easier for the state to reject completed ballots over technicalities. The rules direct county officials to “spoil” mail-in ballots when the inner envelope is not sealed perfectly or when a voter’s signature does clearly match the name of an application number on the return envelope — even if the voter uses a nickname, maiden name or initials.

While election officials typically issue replacement ballots, the plaintiffs argued that voters whose errors are discovered close to Election Day rarely have enough time to submit a new one.

At a recent hearing, the plaintiff’s attorney Jacob Shelly said that most voters simply do not recast ballots after county officials declare them spoiled.

More than 123,000 voters had already submitted requests for absentee ballots as of Oct. 8, and 31,582 had been requested by the Oct. 14 hearing, according to court records. Absentee voting is largely utilized by overseas military service members and elderly and disabled voters. Shelly argued the new instructions lack clear standards and could produce inconsistent treatment across county lines.

“The Board’s new Republican majority rushed to implement eleventh-hour absentee ballot restrictions that will inevitably disenfranchise scores of North Carolina voters,” the plaintiffs argued. “They will invalidate thousands of qualified voters’ ballots in the November election unless enjoined,” the motion added.

Those rules will remain law at least through the midterms, per Schroeder’s Monday ruling.

In the order, the judge makes light of Shelly’s arguments to provide an alternative to the voting rules.

“Plaintiffs’ proposed remedy eliminates any verification of the signature, permitting a voter to sign anyone’s name to the certification, even ‘Mickey Mouse,’” he wrote.

North Carolina’s election board shifted to a 3–2 Republican majority in May 2025 after the state’s Republican auditor, Dave Boliek, gained appointment authority. The board approved the changes despite a state law putting them on hold a week prior, which Democratic Gov. Josh Stein called a “blatant circumvention of the law.”

The board’s messaging around the changes reflected talking points repeated by President Donald Trump, who has claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is unreliable and rife with voter fraud. The Supreme Court recently blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing new rules pushed by the president to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of the midterms.

North Carolina has rolled out increasingly rigid voting rules in recent years. The state passed voter ID laws in 2023, and requiring voters to fill out their ballots in the presence of two witnesses and attach a photo copy of their ID if they intend to vote by mail.

In-person early voting in the state kicked off last Thursday.

entries.title: The Commanders Can't Complete Their Comeback in a Loss to the 49ers
entries.summary: After a lifeless first half, Washington came within a score of undefeated San Francisco in a 23-17 defeat.
entries.content:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Despite being given several opportunities to pull off an improbable win against the undefeated 49ers, the Commanders came up short of a comeback in a 23-17 defeat on Monday Night Football.

Facing a third-and-long from San Francisco’s 40-yard line with six seconds left in the game, quarterback Jayden Daniels was sacked to provide an anticlimactic finish to a game that had plenty of twists and turns.

The Commanders trailed 23-3 midway through the third quarter, but were able to claw back within six points in the fourth. At one point, Washington appeared to take the lead on a long touchdown run from Jeremy McNichols, but it was called back by a penalty.

“I love their fight, but I'm sick about the ending,” coach Dan Quinn said. “When it's hard, I love their resolve. But to be the team that we need to be, we've got to be more consistent.”

Daniels finished 29 of 40 for 300 yards and two touchdowns. Touchdown catches by Stefon Diggs and Rachaad White gave Washington hope, but in the end it wasn’t enough. While the loss drops Washington to 1-4-1, Monday’s late surge marked a dramatic shift from a deflating first half.

The 49ers Christian McCaffrey (64 yards rushing and two touchdowns) and Mike Evans (94 yards receiving) took turns carving up Washington early, helping San Francisco get out to a 20-3 lead by halftime.

Washington’s offense didn’t reach the end zone until there were 15 seconds remaining in the third quarter. Its struggles were made worse by the loss of Pro Bowl receiver Terry McLaurin, who went down with a leg injury in the first quarter. The unit looked rudderless for much of the first half, generating just 90 yards and failing to convert on a third down before the break.

“We dug ourselves a hole,” Daniels said after the loss. “We’ve got to [put together] a full game, be a four-quarter team. You know, not just a half team.”

Washington started to show some signs of life in the third quarter. Daniels found Stefon Diggs for a one-yard touchdown pass and, after forcing a three-and-out on the next 49ers possession, Washington drove 80 yards down the field and scored again to pull within a six points.

But on the Commanders’ final drive, Daniels was pressured into an intentional grounding penalty with 16 seconds remaining, which cost his team a down and a crucial 10 seconds on the clock. Given one last shot at a Hail Mary, two 49er pass rushers combined for a sack as double zeros hit the scoreboard.

entries.title: String of Sexual Misconduct Scandals in the House Hasn’t Fast-tracked Ethics Reform
entries.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson canceled the pre-midterm House session, punting any action on changes to sexual misconduct rules.
entries.content:
Following a string of sexual misconduct scandals in the House earlier this year, lawmakers pledged to overhaul how the chamber — and Congress in general — handles allegations in order to protect staff.

But months have passed since the high-profile resignations of Reps. Eric Swalwell (D-California) and Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) following allegations of misconduct involving congressional aides — and Republican leadership has yet to prioritize any action on stricter ethics rules.

The day before House Speaker Mike Johnson canceled most of the House’s session in September, Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-New Mexico) and Kat Cammack (R-Florida) approached him in the chamber to let him know they wanted to introduce their long-awaited bipartisan ethics reform package before lawmakers left Washington before the election.

But Johnson was noncommittal.

“It hadn't been official that we weren't going to have the time to be able to finalize and do the last bit of work we needed, so I was still pushing for us getting something done,” Leger Fernández told The Washington Sun, recalling the Sept. 2 conversation. “He knew in his mind he was going to cancel. So he was saying, ‘Well, you know, we’ll get something done, but I don’t know.’”

The following morning, House Republican leadership sent out the official notice canceling two weeks of session, giving members more time to hit the campaign trail but cutting legislative business short.

Leger Fernández and Cammack, the chairs of the Democratic and Republican women’s caucuses, respectively, have been working on a legislative package to overhaul how the House addresses sexual misconduct allegations. The joint effort was announced by both Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in May, but it has repeatedly stalled due to the House schedule being cut short this fall.
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)“I repeatedly pointed out that I had thought we should get these done earlier, but the constant breaks and interruptions in the legislative session have meant we haven't been able to finalize the work,” Leger Fernández said.

Leger Fernández said that meant it was difficult to get input from staff: “We kept having to cancel steps that were important to move us forward.”

When House lawmakers return to Washington after the midterms, they will have just 20 legislative days in the Capitol to get anything done. That period is expected to be busy, particularly if Republicans lose the majority in one or both chambers of Congress: Lawmakers have to approve a spending bill since government funding runs out on Dec. 11, negotiate a must-pass Pentagon policy bill, and debate permitting reform and college sports legislation. Republicans are also weighing another reconciliation bill to pass their legislative agenda and extend the debt limit.

Cammack and Leger Fernández expect to introduce a package that would include proposals like prohibiting members from dating staffers (currently, they’re only barred from having romantic relationships with staff in their own offices), updating the Congressional Accountability Act (a law that requires Congress to follow employment laws that apply to the private sector), and creating a “one-stop shop” to make it easier for people to come forward with allegations, Cammack said. Both women’s caucuses have held multiple meetings and listening sessions with male and female staffers and members of Congress to come up with recommendations.

Given the crowded legislative calendar, even supporters pushing for action admit it’s likely to get punted.

“I’m not confident anything’s going to get done when we get back,” Rep. Nancy Mace (R-South Carolina) told The Sun. “It’s going to be a disaster. I mean, we’re going to be trying to get through as much as we can, hopefully, before the end of the year. I don’t know how much of an appetite there is for ethics reform.”

“I don’t think women are taken seriously on the hill. Period,” added Mace, who said she’d personally support the efforts.

A senior House Republican, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, concurred, telling The Sun that the lame-duck business “will more likely dictate” whether ethics reform gets brought to the floor.

Still, Cammack told The Sun that she and Leger Fernández are “committed to getting a product out the door on the floor and passed by the end of this year.”

Cammack recalled that Johnson told her and Leger Fernández “that this is a priority and that he is going to do everything he can to help us make sure that this gets wrapped up by the end of the year.” Johnson’s office did not comment for this story.
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)But Democratic lawmakers pointed to Johnson’s record on issues related to sexual misconduct as a reason why they believe ethics reform will not get done. They noted he refused to bring a bill to the floor to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein, and he took nearly five months after allegations against Gonzales first came out to call on him to not run for reelection. The speaker is also supporting Rep. Max Miller’s (R-Ohio) reelection campaign despite allegations of domestic violence made by his ex-wife, and he dismissed concerns related to Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida) after a judge issued a restraining order against him to protect his ex-girlfriend from “dating violence.”

“Anybody with ethics reform on their bingo card in the lame-duck session from Republicans should go get a new bingo card. It ain’t happening,” said one House Democrat, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “If it does, it would be a shock to the world, and inconsistent with the way the Republicans have led for the last two years.”

A second House Democrat said, “I hope [Cammack] is right. But I’m not holding my breath.”

Jeffries told reporters in late September that there is an “expectation that there is going to be decisive action that Congress takes in a bipartisan way on this issue as soon as we return.” While Johnson has not publicly made any commitments, he has been supportive of some of the measures floated by Cammack and Leger Fernández, such as barring members from having romantic or sexual relationships with congressional staffers.

Members of Congress have pushed for reforms in the next session starting in January. At a House Rules Committee hearing in September for members to make suggestions to the rules package for the upcoming Congress, some lawmakers pushed to ban members from dating any congressional staffer, to update members’ training to prevent sexual misconduct, and to amend members’ code of conduct to ensure there are clear consequences for sexual misconduct, including facing expulsion votes and getting removed from committees.

“We need due process,” Leger Fernández, a House Rules Committee member, said at the hearing.

Some of the provisions in the House package would need Senate action, which Cammack said could add difficulties.

“If I’m being honest, it appears that the Senate seems more intent on passing college sports reforms than actually doing the work that the House has sent them, so that’s pretty frustrating, which is why we’ve also talked about just a rules package that would be [a resolution] that would have impacted the House only, but we know that the issue of sexual misconduct is not exclusive to the House, it’s on Senate side too,” Cammack said.

Both Leger Fernández and Cammack said they haven’t formally introduced a bill because lawmakers haven’t been on Capitol Hill to discuss the details and generate support for it. They considered introducing one during one of the brief pro forma sessions, when one member presides and no significant business is conducted.

“This is about cleaning up the House,” Cammack said. “There’s so many things that people are unaware of. We recognized early on there would be an education campaign, so introducing in a pro forma doesn’t exactly help us in driving that awareness campaign.”

Outside groups pushing for ethics reforms have grown impatient with the delays.

“You’ve had several members who are no longer running for reelection because of the issue, and all of those members have either resigned or have decided not to seek reelection because of public pressure, not because of a process has demanded they leave, but because of the public saying we don’t want these people to come back,” said Emma Davidson Tribbs, founding director of the National Women’s Defense League. “The public wants the system to be adjusted, and, to me, that says that they should be taking this seriously.”
Congress Ethics Swalwell (3777x2518, AR: 1.50)Cheyenne Hunt, founder and executive director of Reckoning Action, told the Sun: “This is a story that women organizers know all too well: Our concerns and things that we take up as important are often put on the back burner.”

“I don’t have a profound amount of faith in Republicans prioritizing this in a lame-duck scenario,” she added.

Hunt, a lawyer and Democratic activist who played a key role in bringing allegations against Swalwell and former Maine Senate Democratic candidate Graham Platner to light, said that she anticipates that any sort of change would take place in the next Congress, where Democrats are expected to have control of at least one chamber. Leger Fernández told The Sun that House Democratic leadership has committed to scheduling a vote on ethics reform next year if they win the majority in November.

The fact that the process has not been prioritized by Republican leadership “sends a clear message to women that there is still very much an old boys club in Washington that is gumming up the gears here to try and make Capitol Hill a safer place to work,” Hunt added.

“That should make all of us uncomfortable,” Hunt continued.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 8
entries.summary: This week’s volleyball standouts include a steady libero, a do-it-all setter and a dominant outside hitter.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

This week’s set of standouts prove that anyone can make a difference on the volleyball court, no matter their position. Here are three locals who got the job done for their teams in a busy Week 8:

Mia Cheng, Senior, Libero, Clarksburg

Cheng, a three-year starter, is the engine driving the Coyotes through another strong regular season. Last week, her steady defensive play at libero helped Clarksburg beat Churchill and Poolesville, two of the best offensive teams in Montgomery County.

The wins helped coach Dawn Dickinson’s team clinch its division for the fourth year in a row. With just four games left in the regular season, Cheng and the Coyotes are well positioned to make a run out of the Maryland 4A West region. They also have a shot to make the county championship game in a few weeks.

“She totally takes control of the back row and the defense,” Dickinson said. “She’s just really stepped up and taken it upon herself to help the other players.”

Ayla Sayd, Senior, Outside Hitter, Marshall

Sayd produced an eye-popping stat line last week against Langley. In a back-and-forth, five-set slugfest on the road, Sayd tallied a season-high 33 kills in a victory. Her final two kills were the most important — with the Statesmen holding a slim 13-12 lead in the fifth set, Sayd’s 32nd and 33rd kills put the match away.

The victory avenged a 3-1 loss to the Saxons in late September. Sayd, an Elon commit, has finished with double-digit kills in every match she’s played this season and is up to 348 putaways on the year.

Jadyn Witt, Senior, Setter, Douglass

Before Douglass kicked off its volleyball campaign, Witt approached coach Tai Heath to request a position change. Her sophomore year, she played outside hitter for the Eagles. Last year, she transitioned to libero. This year, she wanted to try out the setter position.

“She’s very even-keeled, so I didn’t even question it,” Heath said. “If she wants to try setting she’s going to be perfectly fine. … I trust her.”

Heath’s trust in Witt has paid off for Douglass, which boasts an undefeated record. Her passing ability has helped the Eagles become one of the most dangerous offenses in Prince George’s County — Heath’s team has dropped just one set so far this season. In a recent bout against College Park Academy, Witt posted six assists, seven aces, five digs and three kills in a dominant three-set sweep.

entries.title: Polymarket Defended Its ‘Cornell Seven’ Trading Market — Then Took It Down
entries.summary: Congressional lawmakers criticized the prediction firm for initially permitting the bets.
entries.content:
The prediction market Polymarket has taken down a page allowing users to bet on the outcome of the “Cornell Seven” gang rape allegations, a reversal that followed public criticism from advocates for survivors’ rights.

On Sept. 30, Polymarket began allowing traders to predict whether the seven men accused in the Cornell University fraternity case would be criminally charged with a felony sex crime by January 2027. By Monday, traders had placed more than $450,000 in bets on the outcome, with more than 70% of users predicting there would not be charges.

In a statement to Front Office Sports, a publication focused on sports news, Polymarket initially defended the page, arguing that "markets bring better, unbiased information about important events, in contrast to the disinformation we’re all drowning in, which too often leaves the public misled and disillusioned to the point of apathy."

However, after Front Office Sports published a story and The Washington Sun requested comment, Polymarket reversed itself and removed the bet as an option.

Polymarket declined to comment when asked to explain why it reversed course.

The decision reflects the mounting scrutiny facing the prediction market industry. Polymarket has largely avoided regulatory scrutiny along with other online gambling companies, and it has hired the president's son Donald Trump Jr. as a strategic adviser as part of a broader Washington lobbying blitz.

However, congressional officials in both parties expressed concern about the “Cornell Seven” betting page in interviews with The Washington Sun.

“Prediction markets have existed for centuries, and there is an underlying logic to them. They proved more accurate in 2024 than the presidential polling,” said Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pennsylvania), a member of the House Ways and Means Committee. “However, like with any market, there also needs to be sensible regulation.”

Similarly, Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) said the option reflected that online gambling has gone too far.

“A proper country recognized the dangers of gambling,” Roy said. “Our nation today is embracing it and fails to realize they’re not watching the car wreck — they’re in it.”

Kalshi, Polymarket’s main competitor, said in a statement that it would not have allowed bets on the outcome of the case. It has banned gambling on missile strikes, kidnappings, deaths and rocket explosions.

It is unlikely that prediction markets will face much federal scrutiny anytime soon. The Federal Trade Commission recently began probing whether online sports gambling companies such as FanDuel and DraftKings promote deceptive or misleading advertisements. That probe is not expected to include the prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, which have been regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, led by a Trump appointee largely seen as supportive of industry.

Opponents of online gambling say the trading page on Cornell reflects the need for the companies to find ever more outlandish topics for bets to keep users entertained and on their platforms.

“You literally can gamble on anything right now, on the most perverse thing you can imagine,” said Les Bernal, the national director of Stop Predatory Gambling. “They’re constantly trying to keep people engaged constantly — every minute, every few seconds, so they continue to wager on these platforms.”

The Cornell trading page was also condemned by I Have the Right To, an advocacy group for survivors of sexual assault.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Show Me the Money
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 20, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A nine-hour D.C. Council hearing, a driverless Metro and the Commanders in prime time. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. Beautiful day on the way, but dry air with brisk breezes may trigger a few fall allergy sneezes. Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

Death and taxes are the only certainties in life. But whether D.C. imposes new taxes on its residents and businesses is still up in the air.

Last week the D.C. Council held a nine-hour hearing on a range of ideas to bring in more revenue, just as the city faces an economic and budget crunch that could threaten a variety of existing programs and services.

Despite a lively debate on everything from new taxes on capital gains to higher property levies for expensive homes that sit vacant most of the year, The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports that lawmakers likely emerged from the hearing realizing that there’s no silver bullet to the city’s fiscal challenges over the next year.

Some proposed tax hikes could be imposed quickly, but may only produce enough revenue to close an existing budget gap. More expansive options could take years to implement while raising concerns about what signal it sends to skittish businesses, investors and people choosing where in the Washington region they should live.

More takeaways from the hearing: A new tax on law firms and lobbyists may sound fair in principle but complicated in reality, and soaking the rich is easy politics but may be counterproductive for a city whose economy needs every boost it can get.

If there was one thing that most people at the hearing agreed on, it’s that D.C. needs a better way to dig into spending and revenue.





DEEP DIVE

Metro’s driverless future: Speaking to a crowd of transit experts last week, WMATA’s general manager, Randy Clarke, addressed the Red Line modernization project, which is expected to fully automate the system’s busiest line at a cost of $1.6 billion, according to the Federal Transit Administration.

“Driverless Metro does not mean we won’t have staff,” Clarke said at the Mobility Forum, a weekly seminar led by MIT professor Jinhua Zhao. He added that Metro has plans to have a “staffing concept of operation” within a year and a half.

It’s just one of the ways the agency is relying on new technology to manage its operations, The Sun’s Will Hofmann reports.

With $2.1 million in funding from Google, MIT’s Transit Lab — led by Zhao — is set to partner with WMATA to build an “open-source agentic AI platform for public transportation monitoring, control, and rider communications.”

WMATA has seen the acceleration of AI as “required” to modernize its transit ecosystem, even recently modifying a contract with Replicant Solutions, an AI-driven customer service vendor, by $3 million. The expanded contract would reflect that a “greater volume of calls has shifted to the AI platform” replacing “more expensive human agent-handled calls,” Fifi Magosi, a WMATA vice president, said at the agency’s Oct. 8 meeting.





FROM THE DISTRICT

No such thing as a coincidence: The federal judge in the East Potomac case is not buying the Trump administration’s argument that its recent mass tree-cutting at the park is disconnected from the president’s recently announced plans for a new championship golf course on site, The Associated Press reports.

“There is no universe in which all of this coincidentally happened all at the same time,” U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said during a Monday hearing.

Reyes previously ordered that the government halt all work at the park until at least next week. While President Donald Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social that golf course architect Tom Fazio will begin the redevelopment on Nov. 15, the government’s lawyers said Monday that there “is not a contract” with Fazio or his company, The Sun’s Reese Gorman reports.

A National Guard member was shot in the leg late Sunday night while attempting to break up a fight near Capitol Hill’s Eastern Market, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

The interim Metropolitan Police chief, Jeffery Carroll, said on Monday that a person was shot in the abdomen after firing their gun toward a group of seven or eight guard members responding to the fight. The suspected shooter and guard member were each transported to the hospital with injuries not considered life-threatening.

A fire destroyed the dining room of La Bonne Vache, a French bistro in Georgetown, on Sunday night, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. The fire displaced two adults who lived above the restaurant.

The Justice Department is investigating whether D.C.’s Department of Corrections “engages in a pattern or practice of violating the constitutional rights” of people incarcerated in its facilities, Kendall reports. The announcement comes days after six people filed a lawsuit claiming they were repeatedly served food with dead mice and bugs while being held at the D.C. jail.

Betting on tech: Mayor Muriel Bowser announced she’ll support 112 local tech start-ups with more than $5 million in funding for training, networking and even (for some) free office space to grow D.C.’s tech economy. The mayor also released a report projecting that local tech jobs will increase by nearly 8% through 2028.

A recent wave of crime committed by teens has reignited debate over how to punish and rehabilitate young offenders, City Cast D.C. reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam’s office received an “envelope containing a suspicious substance,” according to a Monday news release. The Virginia lawmaker, who’s running for reelection in the state’s 10th Congressional District, denounced the letter as “political intimidation” that has “no place in our country.” His office joined a list of several congressional offices that received letters containing unknown substances.





FROM THE DINING ROOM

The most important meal of the day: Sun food correspondent Tom Sietsema ranked his five favorite breakfasts in the D.C. area, highlighting everything from a crab cake and eggs platter inside Eastern Market to a picture-perfect stack of pancakes in Arlington.

SPORTS

49ers 23, Commanders 17: In a game of two very distinct halves, the Commanders came out flat but showed some fight after the break. Despite losing Terry McLaurin to a leg injury, the offense found a rhythm and Jayden Daniels threw two touchdowns to pull Washington within a score. But two late drives came up of the end zone, and the Commanders will head into their bye week at 1-4-1. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson breaks down the good and the bad from Week 6.

The Wizards kick off a new season tomorrow, hosting the Bucks at Capital One. The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports that outside expectations for the team are mixed this year, as many league sources and national media outlets aren’t sure how the team’s new veterans will work with its young core.

“They have to prove they can win,” one executive told The Sun. “Do the young guys know how to do that?”

One undeniable bright spot for Washington? No. 1 overall pick AJ Dybantsa. But Alex reports that the buzzy rookie may not suit up Wednesday as he’s still considered day-to-day with an ankle injury.

Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was C) National Harbor. That is the new home of “The Awakening.” A special shout-out to Nancy Ward, who answered first.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Words and Actions
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Democrats’ investigations promise. The rising costs of MAGA merch. Who’s coming to Crooked Con. New McConnell-isms. Polymarket bets wrong. Don’t bet on House ethics reform this year.





THE LATEST

Promises, promises: “If Democrats win back the House, I’ll become Chairman — and I’ll have subpoena power,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California), the ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, said in an August small-dollar fundraising appeal. Gotta win first though, he went on, pleading for at least $5 with the promise of investigations galore to follow.

The Washington Sun’s Stephen Neukam pored over a plethora of fundraising emails to find that the promise to investigate Donald Trump’s administration, family deals and much, much more have been a huge part of the Democratic pitch for cash.

Stephen points out that the House Ethics Manual prohibits tying campaign contribution solicitations to actions taken or expected to be taken in a lawmaker’s official capacity. (“No comment,” said Tom Rust, staff director and chief counsel to the House Ethics Committee.)

There are also some political questions here: Leaning way into the party base’s dreams and fears is a time-honored part of grassroots fundraising. Just $5 and all your political enemies will be vanquished, allowing the light of truth to shine brightly for all time*.

(*all time = a year or so until the next cycle starts up.)

If Democrats do take control of the House, how much time should they devote to making good on that $5 promise? The Sun’s Alex Roarty reports on some exclusive polling from centrist Democratic group Third Way that suggests the answer is not that much. Some 27% of voters think Democrats “should prioritize investigating Trump for misconduct and impeaching the president if he has broken the law,” the poll found, while 68% said Democrats should “prioritize bringing down costs for the American people, not investigations and impeachment.”

But after firing up the base, what should Democrats actually do? “It’s not like if they don’t take any type of political advantage of this, the Republicans aren’t going to go, ‘Oh, this is really good oversight. We’re glad you’re doing this,’” Kurt Bardella, a senior comms guy for the Texas Democratic Party, told The Sun’s Manuela Silva. “Like, that’s not going to happen.”

Bardella is unique among Democrats in that he used to be the messaging guy for an orgy of House Republican Oversight investigations when he worked for Rep. Darrell Issa years ago. He said Issa also raised plenty of money with the GOP base off the promise of investigations, but he also remembers Issa not being singularly focused on Barack Obama. (Obama vets may remember this differently.) Bardella’s advice to Garcia: Investigate a lot of stuff, all over the place, to try to convince the public you’re not just in this for the fundraising dollars. “We went after so many things that weren’t partisan,” Bardella said. “Just good government shit.”

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


MAGA hat-flation: Trump’s iconic red hat embroidered with “Make America Great Again” sold for $25 on DonaldJTrump.com when he first ran for president in 2015. On Jan. 6, 2021, it cost $30. Today’s version for sale on The Trump Organization’s online storefront retails for $55 — a 120% increase from 2015. (The hat is $40 on the president’s political site.) The Sun’s Nicole Belcastro combed through many MAGA items for sale and has charts — charts! — showing similar price hikes through the years.

First on The Sun: Rep. Ilhan Omar to appear at Crooked Con. The rising Democratic confab, centered around the empire built by the Pod Save boys, is adding a flurry of new speakers to the roster today, representing the differing and often squabbling sides of the party. Omar, whom the Trump administration is looking into deporting, will be there from the party’s left, as will prominent voices from the Democratic center. Sen. Chris Murphy and Reps. Robert Garcia, Sara Jacobs and Yassamin Ansari are also among the electeds who have newly signed on. The whole thing kicks off in D.C. two days after the midterms, so Democrats will be either in a great mood … or a really, really terrible mood.

FROM THE PREDICTION MARKETS


They didn’t predict this? On Sept. 30, Polymarket began allowing trades on whether the seven men accused in the Cornell fraternity case would be criminally charged with a felony sex crime by January 2027. Cue the outrage anyone could have expected, and then the surprising pushback: “Markets bring better, unbiased information about important events, in contrast to the disinformation we’re all drowning in,” Polymarket told Front Office Sports of the haters. What comes next? If you bet the walkback, congratulations, you have been around the block a couple times.

After The Sun’s Jeff Stein asked for comment on the Cornell listing, Polymarket reversed and removed it as an option. The company declined to comment on the change, though.

Inevitable knife-twist: Kalshi, Polymarket’s main competitor, said in a statement that it would not have allowed bets on the outcome of the case.



FROM THE HILL


What irks Mitch McConnell about Trump: The AP’s Michael Tackett is out with an updated version of his McConnell biography in paperback, which includes new interviews with the senator from Kentucky. Trump “seems to be very approving of monetizing his influence,” McConnell told Tackett. The former Republican Senate leader “could not abide Trump being portrayed as Jesus in social media posts,” Tackett writes. McConnell also said the president is wrong to publicly criticize the Supreme Court: “I don’t know what he expected,” McConnell said, “... They don’t report to him.”

Bonus annoyance: “The Department of Defense is the name of the organization,” McConnell said of Trump’s Department of War.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Ethics reform stalls out: You may recall that, approximately a million years ago in news time, the resignations of Reps. Eric Swalwell and Tony Gonzales amid ugly sexual misconduct allegations involving staff were going to force ethics reform in the House. The Sun’s Oriana González reports that in the intervening time, momentum behind reform has gone the way of the dinosaur. The two women spearheading the push, Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-New Mexico) and Kat Cammack (R-Florida), disagree slightly about their chances in the lame-duck session after the midterms. But Oriana reports that the feeling on the Hill is that there likely won’t be time for it.

entries.title: Inflation Hits Trump’s Merch Machine
entries.summary: It’s costing more to look and smell like Donald Trump.
entries.content:
The economy is reeling from inflation, tariffs, and a war in Iran that’s made it more expensive to fill your gas tank, fridge and closet.

The Trump economy is also affecting Trump merch: The cost of Make America Great Again hats and several other Trump-themed items have spiked as well.

A Washington Sun review of dozens of Trump products, sold across several digital storefronts operated by the president’s political committees and private business ventures, revealed notable price hikes for several popular products.

Trump’s iconic red hat embroidered with “Make America Great Again” sold for $25 on DonaldJTrump.com when Trump first ran for president in 2015.
Trump.MAGA.hat (2251x1501, AR: 1.50)Just before Trump left the White House, the price of official MAGA hats had inched up to $30, The Washington Sun found through a WayBack Machine capture on January 6, 2021.

Today’s version for sale on the Trump Organization’s online storefront retails for $55 — a 120% increase from the cap’s 2015 price. The U.S. inflation rate rose 41% over the same time period, according to the Federal Reserve.

Trump’s political website, which sells “official Trump merchandise,” is offering the same hat for $40.

MAGA hats have been a particularly notable profit driver for Trump’s business and political operations: Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, said Trump’s 2016 campaign sold up to $80,000 a day worth of MAGA hats. In 2024, Trump officials told The Independent the campaign had shipped more than 2 million MAGA hats since the start of 2023.

Smelling Trumpesque also costs more than it used to: Trump’s “Victory 47” perfume has risen in price twice since February 2024, for a total increase of $150.

The “sophisticated” and “subtly feminine” perfume cost $99 when it debuted on the Trump Sneakers website, before it was redesigned and repriced to feature a miniature Trump atop the bottle for $199.

Now, “Victory 47” costs $249 — or buy two and save $100 — and features a slightly larger miniature Trump. The fragrance’s promise to capture “confidence, beauty, and unstoppable determination” remains the same.
Trump.Fragrances (2294x1878, AR: 1.22)Another set of Trump offerings — gold and silver medallions featuring the president’s face — fluctuate by the minute. The retail price changes appear tied to the spot prices of silver and gold, meaning they can increase or decrease by tens or even hundreds of dollars in a matter of weeks. Gold bullion prices remain near historic highs, while silver remains above historic averages.

The White House directed the Sun’s questions to the Trump Organization, which didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Trump has regularly denied he personally profits from elected office.

A higher merch price tag is irrelevant to most Trump supporters, who will pay any price to signal “allegiance to somebody who they think is tough, somebody who they think says the types of things that other people aren't willing to say,” said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University in Washington, D.C.

MAGA supporters’ willingness to spend almost anything for Trump-related products helps the president fuel his extensive political apparatus while also personally profiting. Trump’s estimated personal income hit $2.2 billion during 2025, according to The New York Times.

Bruce Newman, a marketing professor for DePaul University’s Driehaus College of Business, says Trump has marketed himself as a brand starting from his time in real estate through his transition to television, and finally, to his time in the White House. Newman believes the president dons the MAGA cap to appear young, strong and confident. “It’s kind of like a baby hanging onto a blanket for a reason of security,” he said.
Trump.bears (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)Both Newman and Belt said they believe customers purchase Trump merchandise to feel like they’re part of a club. This need, they said, overrides concerns they may have about the rising cost of food, gasoline, housing and other necessities.

Nevertheless, Belt calls the Trump merch price increases “tone-deaf,” especially given higher demand during an election cycle where affordability is a top concern for 84% of voters, according to the Pew Research Center.The prices of some prominent Trump products have remained steady since he returned to the White House last year.

Those include golf and pickleball clothing collections, a “Golden Age” candle, chocolate bars wrapped to look like Trump engraved gold bars and treats packaged in clear plastic bags topped with “Trump Sweets” stickers.
Trump.God.Bless.The.USA.Bible (7855x5237, AR: 1.50)Trump also licenses his name to peddle products, most notably the “God Bless the USA” bible. The president has encouraged those looking to “Make America Pray Again” to purchase the bibles, which he co-markets with country musician Lee Greenwood.

The original “God Bless the USA” bible has consistently sold for $59.99, while an edition to that bible called “The Day God Intervened” has sold for $69.99. But newer, pricier bibles are now on sale, including the $74.99 “Camo Edition,” the $99.99 “Platinum Edition” and the $99.99 “America 250 Edition.”
Trump.MAGA.hat.graphic (1308x1150, AR: 1.14)No presidential family has profited off the presidency as much as Trump’s family, Forbes reported.
Trump.Medallion (1316x786, AR: 1.67)Connecting customers to Trump-related history is a prevalent marketing strategy in his second-term selling.

With the purchase of a Trump-themed digital trading card, for example, buyers will receive a swatch of Trump’s “Knockout Suit” — the navy blue suit he wore during the June 2024 debate against then-President Joe Biden, who ended his reelection bid a month later.

“That's trying to get all the sales you can before you leave office. Donald Trump knows that his political career is on the clock, and he's going to try to get as much out of it financially as he possibly can,” Belt said.

entries.title: What NBA Execs, Experts and Oddsmakers Are Saying About the Wizards
entries.summary: Ahead of Wednesday’s opener, we compiled a range of opinions on the Wizards’ outlook this season.
entries.content:
The new-look Washington Wizards open their season Wednesday against the Milwaukee Bucks, and the organization is looking to do something it hasn’t in recent years: win.

After years of tanking, the Wizards enter the season with the expectation that they will be competitive under coach Brian Keefe. Veterans Trae Young and Anthony Davis and No. 1 overall draft pick AJ Dybantsa (who is day-to-day with an ankle sprain and may miss the season opener) have been added to a young, inexperienced core, giving fans more reason for optimism than in the past several years.

But it’s no guarantee that the Wizards will be immediate players in a competitive Eastern Conference. Here’s how experts around the league are viewing Washington’s chances.

Around the League

The Washington Sun reached out to multiple NBA front-office executives across the league to get their opinions on the Wizards. The executives were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the Wizards since they don’t have permission to talk publicly about other teams.

The consensus was that while the roster is clearly more talented, it’s unclear if that can translate to a winning record.

“They have to prove they can win,” one executive told The Sun. “Do the young guys know how to do that?”

Another executive compared them to another local team coming out of a rebuild in the Washington Nationals, who outplayed expectations in the first half of the season but elected to stick with their young core (and traded away some veterans for future assets at the trade deadline) instead of competing for a Wild Card berth.

“They could overachieve in the first half of the season and still be sellers at the deadline,” the executive said. “If they win 44 games but Trae Young and AD are the main reasons why and not the young guys, is that a good season? But if the young guys take a major step forward and they’re trading Davis and some veterans at the deadline to give AJ and co. the keys at the cost of making the Play-In, isn’t that better?”

A third executive was higher on the roster than most.

“I think they’re onto something,” the third executive said. “They have an abundance of elite wings and youth; you can’t get enough of either in today’s NBA. AJ is a franchise player, and they’re huge — enough size to protect Trae on defense, and all of their young guys have improved. The roster is a little weird, but there’s enough there to where it might just work.”

The third executive disagreed with the second’s assessment of the trade deadline, adding that if Washington has a shot at the postseason it should do everything it can to get there after years of irrelevance.

“They should want to make the Play-In Tournament,” the executive said. “That feels like a reasonable goal.”

The league's annual GM survey also gave the Wizards some recognition. The team finished second to the Pacers for which team GMs think will be most improved, with 23% of the vote, while Dybantsa tied with Chicago’s Caleb Wilson for which rookie will be the best player in five years (both received 33% of the vote).

From the Media

The Wizards open the season in the bottom third of The Athletic’s power rankings and are projected to finish the season 11th in the Eastern Conference and miss the playoffs. While acknowledging an improvement in talent, The Athletic cites the potential lack of cohesion, shooting and playmaking outside of Young as factors that could derail the season.

ESPN ranks Washington an identical 22nd in its power rankings, while The Ringer views the Wizards’ prospects as much bleaker, placing them 28th in its power rankings. The outlet called the Wizards “a disgracefully impatient excuse for a basketball team” and questioned the decisions to add veterans such as Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton to a young roster.

The Oddsmakers

The sportsbooks also don’t expect much from the Wizards this season. Both DraftKings and FanDuel have the Wizards’ odds of winning the NBA championship at 150-to-1 to open the season, while BetMGM has the Wizards’ over/under for wins at 34.5.

FanDuel has the Wizards’ odds of avoiding the Play-In Tournament and clinching the sixth seed in the Eastern Conference at 22-to-1 and their odds of clinching the eighth seed and final spot in the playoffs at 13-to-1.

entries.title: Five Takeaways From the D.C. Council’s Big Hearing on New Taxes
entries.summary: Lawmakers and experts are split on whether the answer to D.C.’s challenging economic situation is asking the wealthy to pay a bigger share or limiting spending.
entries.content:
Last Friday, the D.C. Council held a nine-hour hearing on the exact thing most taxpayers never want to hear about: possible tax increases.

The discussion came amid challenging economic times in the city, and ahead of a significant political change in D.C. that will see a new mayor take office in January. A range of experts and advocates made their pitch to the council, some urging lawmakers to make the wealthy pay a bigger share and others countering that now is the time to limit existing spending.

We wouldn’t expect you to sit through the entire hearing yourself, so here are our main takeaways.

There’s no silver bullet — at least not a quick one.

This much was undisputed leading into and during Friday’s hearing: D.C. is facing a deficit next year of anywhere between $600 and $800 million in a roughly $11 billion local budget.

While some lawmakers argued that existing spending needed to be scrutinized, the hearing itself was an indication that a number of council members believe that some types of taxes may have to be raised next year.

But even advocates of the idea likely came away from the hearing understanding that there aren’t many workable options that could quickly raise revenue — and the ones that exist would only pull in enough extra cash to fill the expected hole, not fund much else beyond it.

“A word of caution: The reality is the financial proposals on the table … are unlikely to support massive new spending programs,” said Ward 5 Council member Zachary Parker. “We need to continue to do the hard work of improving our procurement systems to deliver better results and cut bloated spending in the budget.”

Of the tax-hike ideas that could bring in substantially more money, aides to D.C. CFO Glen Lee made clear that implementing those wouldn’t happen overnight — in fact, they warned, it could take between 12 and 24 months.

None of this is to say that taxes would be increased next year. On Monday, Chair Phil Mendelson noted that the budget for the current fiscal year was $1 billion leaner than the year prior. “We were able to move forward without a major tax increase,” he said.

Whether to raise taxes next year, he added, will be a political choice, not an undeniable necessity. But with anywhere from two to four new lawmakers joining the council between January and early summer, Mendelson may well find himself in the minority.

There was a lot of talk about taxing law firms and lobbyists — but it’s complicated.

There’s not a ton of political sympathy out there for lawyers or lobbyists, so it’s easy to understand how a tax proposal targeting them would seem like an easy sell. The reality, of course, is much more complicated.

For years, some advocates in D.C. have called on the city to impose what’s known as a Business Activity Tax, or a new levy that would hit law firms, lobbying shops and consultancies owned by nonresidents who can claim all the profit as personal income, thus allowing them to avoid paying the city’s usual business taxes. Proponents say it’s a matter of simple fairness: If a normal business operating in D.C. has to pay business taxes, why should a law firm owned by someone who lives in Maryland get to skip out? (Layered on top of this is another unfair reality, they add: Congress has prohibited D.C. from taxing the income of nonresidents.)

“This moment isn’t about maintaining the status quo or kicking the can down the road. It means taking a hard look at who contributes to [government] services and who our tax code lets off the hook,” said Ward 4 Council member Janeese Lewis George, who is expected to be D.C.’s next mayor and during her campaign endorsed imposing a Business Activity Tax in order to fund her plan to bring down the cost of child care.

Advocates say a 2% BAT could bring in $500 million a year and broaden the city’s tax base, making it more resistant to periodic economic ups and downs. They also say it’s not an outlandish proposal: New Hampshire has had one for years without apparent negative impacts to the state’s business climate.

Critics, though, warned that any tax that targets lawyers is likely to end up in court, potentially delaying the revenue it promises to bring in. Additionally, past efforts to impose a BAT envisioned it as part of a broader revenue-neutral package, where the new tax could be largely offset by decreases in other business taxes.

Finally, former Mayor Anthony Williams cautioned that in a moment where D.C.’s commercial property values continue falling, taking aim at lawyers and lobbyists who may still have offices in downtown D.C. isn’t a particularly wise move. “I think we’re just making it harder for some firms that are a key component of the office economy to stay in D.C.,” he said. “That’s not a risk worth taking.”

Eat the rich — or not?

While the council could consider any type of tax increase, it’s been clear that the goal is to target D.C.’s wealthiest households.

Ward 1 Council member Brianne Nadeau wants to impose a 3% surcharge on capital gains, piggybacking on an existing federal tax. The tax would target individuals making more than $400,000 a year, or couples pulling in north of $500,000. The total take: an estimated $200 million a year in new revenue. And Ward 3 Council member Matt Frumin has proposed a pied-à-terre tax, essentially a higher property tax rate on homes worth more than $2.5 million that aren’t occupied by their owner year-round.

“The goal is simple: Protect ordinary wages and ensure that those who receive substantial returns from accumulated wealth contribute fairly to the city we all depend on,” said Nadeau.

Lee, the city’s CFO, cautioned that D.C.’s wealthiest residents already shoulder a significant share of the city’s tax burden. Just over 12,000 people — 3.5% of all taxpayers — contributed more than $1.4 billion to the city’s tax coffers in 2024, or 42% of the city’s total take that year. Additionally, they’re also positioned to find clever ways to avoid higher taxes if any new ones are imposed.

Opinions were split on whether higher taxes would push wealthy residents to leave D.C., especially since lower-tax Virginia is just over the Potomac River. Some experts said research points to some tax flight happening, while others said it would be minimal or nonexistent.

But Williams said that by increasing taxes, whether on wealthy individuals or some businesses, lawmakers would be sending the wrong signal to people it should be looking to keep, as well as people it could be looking to attract. Instead, he said, the council and new mayor should develop some type of “grand compromise” that focuses on a combination of spending cuts, some tax breaks for businesses and incremental tax increases that are broadly applied.

“Everyone is coming to the table and giving up something for the greater good,” he said. “The council can send a powerful signal that will trigger economic growth.”

Raising the sales tax or property taxes will be a tougher sell.

While taxing law firms and wealthy homeowners got the most attention, lawmakers have also been considering broader tax hikes, including by raising the city’s existing sales tax by a percentage point or imposing an across-the-board increase on property taxes.

“We are going to have to do something courageous in the next budget,” said Elissa Silverman, an at-Large council member.

Many of her colleagues said they’d want to avoid across-the-board tax increases, largely because they could disproportionately impact lower-income residents. That’s especially the case with the D.C. sales tax, which Mayor Muriel Bowser has pushed to increase to 7% from the current 6%.

Still, Mendelson said on Monday that the council should think about tax hikes that hit everyone, not just the wealthy. And that could start with increasing the city’s sales tax, since the underlying rationale would be to create a more reliable funding stream for the Metro. “I do think that some of the negatives have been overstated,” he said of a sales tax increase.

There was one point of agreement: D.C. needs a better way.

While lawmakers and others who spoke at the hearing differed on the particulars of various tax hikes — and whether tax increases were even necessary — there was something of a consensus that D.C.’s current process for digging into spending and raising revenue isn’t working.

Consider: Friday’s hearing was the council’s first dedicated deep dive into tax policy in as long as anyone could remember, and every time lawmakers have increased taxes in recent years, it’s happened at the last-minute during the budget process, with little chance for residents to explore benefits and drawbacks.

“There’s a better way to do this,” said Nadeau.

Some lawmakers are pushing for the council to create a new commission that would be empowered to dig into city spending and tax proposals; others simply want Mendelson to revive the council’s finance and revenue committee, which he disbanded six years ago.

“It may be worth us looking at a neutral body that can look at government spending and produce recommendations,” said Parker.

D.C. did have the Tax Revision Commission, which was supposed to meet once a decade and produce recommendations for making the city’s tax code more equitable and competitive, but it imploded in 2024 over disagreements about implementing a Business Activity Tax.

entries.title: Trump Voters Are Souring on Trump, Says a New Survey
entries.summary: A center-left think tank’s latest survey finds trouble for Republicans — alongside warnings for Democrats.
entries.content:
One-third of voters who supported President Donald Trump in 2024 think his presidency is going worse than expected, according to a new poll — a worrying sign for Republicans as they try to save the party’s congressional majorities ahead of next month’s election.

The survey from the center-left Democratic think tank Third Way found that the share of Trump voters who thought things were going worse than expected had swelled from 22% in their April survey to 33% in September, when the new poll was conducted.

Overall, 56% of all voters in the survey said they thought Trump’s presidency was going worse than expected. Just 16% of them said it was going better than they thought it would.

The poll’s results are part of a flurry of public opinion data showing Trump’s poor standing with the electorate, with some surveys showing his approval ratings slipping to the mid-30s. The president’s popularity has been a major issue in this year’s election, which has seen GOP candidates on the defensive in House and Senate seats once deemed safely Republican.

Third Way’s survey leaves little doubt about the primary reason for Trump’s sagging approval ratings: the economy. Ninety percent of voters in the survey say the country is experiencing high inflation; another 55% of voters say the country is in a recession.

The survey is Third Way’s fifth installment of its Signal series, which officials with the group have designed to help guide the Democratic Party’s messaging both before and after the midterm election.

In addition to worrying news for Republicans, the latest poll also contains a warning for Democrats who hope a Democratic-controlled Congress aggressively confronts the president. Twenty-seven percent of voters think Democrats “should prioritize investigating Trump for misconduct and impeaching the president if he has broken the law,” the poll found, while 68% said Democrats should “prioritize bringing down costs for the American people, not investigations and impeachment.”

The survey also found much broader support for policies like auditing the federal government than implementing single-payer health care, a favorite of progressives.

The poll surveyed 2,000 registered voters from Sept. 17 through Sept. 24. It was conducted by the Democratic polling firm GBAO.

Whether you’re a tinkerer, a collector or just have a household full of drivers, your wish list may be topped by a big garage. Unlike car culture meccas like Los Angeles, where there are about 80 properties currently listed for sale with garage parking for six or more cars, the D.C. region isn’t overflowing with garages. entries.title: Trump Probes Are Becoming a Cash Cow for Democrats
entries.summary: A Washington Sun analysis found House Democrats are using promises to investigate the president and his family to solicit campaign contributions.
entries.content:
Investigating President Trump, his family and allies has turned into an increasingly popular fundraising pitch for some Democrats, who in recent months have dangled the probes as a lure for campaign contributions.

California Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the investigative House Oversight Committee, sent an August fundraising email appeal to supporters with the subject line “Subpoena power,” saying that as chair of the panel, he was prepared to compel testimony from members of the president’s family and inner circle.

“If Democrats win back the House, I’ll become Chairman — and I’ll have subpoena power,” Garcia wrote in the message to supporters. “The power to subpoena Trump’s family, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Todd Blanche, and everyone involved in the Epstein files.”

But first, the email said, Democrats must win the House, so he asked donors to contribute $5 to help the party win the majority.

Democrats have made accountability for Trump, his administration and family a central part of their midterms pitch to voters. Leaders in both the House and Senate focused heavily on Trump’s corruption in the year before the election, and Garcia told The Washington Sun in June about his investigative plans if he became chairman of the Oversight Committee.

The fundraising tactic adds an ethical question to the promises from Democrats: The lawmakers seeking to run the investigations are also using them to raise money for their political operation.

The House Ethics Manual prohibits tying campaign contribution solicitations to actions taken or expected to be taken in a lawmaker's official capacity.

The House Ethics Committee declined to explain how it interprets or enforces congressional rules prohibiting lawmakers from linking campaign contribution solicitations to official actions.

Asked whether the rules distinguish between fundraising on a broader oversight agenda and soliciting donations while pledging specific investigations or subpoenas, Tom Rust, the committee’s staff director and chief counsel, replied: “No comment.”

The fundraising appeals reviewed by The Sun do not cross an ethical line, according to Kedric Payne, a former deputy chief counsel at the Office of Congressional Ethics.

Payne said the solicitations are no different from, for example, a candidate promising to repeal Obamacare while asking for supporters to contribute to their campaign.

“That’s just part of the reason that you want people to support you, because you’re going into office to do something,” Payne said.

Instead, the House ethics rules are concerned with lawmakers soliciting campaign contributions from donors who have direct interest in a specific official action, Payne said.

“The Ethics rule comes in to get those things that are in the gray where your intent may not be so corrupt to get you under the bribery standard, but you clearly are asking for a campaign contribution from certain people that they might think is tied to certain official acts,” Payne said.

Garcia is the most prolific of the Democrats fundraising off the promise to launch Trump probes. The Sun analysis of archived emails collected by the Archive of Political Emails, a publicly accessible database of political fundraising messages by the nonprofit Defending Democracy Together, found a few dozen similar emails, primarily from Garcia, but also several other Democrats on the Oversight Committee — Reps. Dave Min of California, Ro Khanna of California, Yassamin Ansari of Arizona and James Walkinshaw of Virginia. The list is not exhaustive, but in all those identified, Democrats ask for contributions to their own campaigns or to party committees, promising to investigate Trumpworld.

“Donald Trump and his family have treated the White House like a personal ATM,” said another fundraising email from Garcia late last month. “That’s why I’m asking you to contribute $5 before our most important fundraising deadline: midnight.

“As the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, I’m prepared to investigate the profiteering, expose the cover-ups, find the records, and drag the people responsible before Congress.”

Of the 32 fundraising emails in the archive that invoked the prospect of investigating the administration and Trump associates, the California Democrat’s campaign sent 28. The count includes repeated solicitations built around similar messages.

The other Democrats each sent one qualifying email. Walkinshaw told supporters in a September fundraising pitch that Democrats would gain the power to investigate and issue subpoenas if they win.

“Here's my message to Donald Trump: Save everything, because we’re coming for it,” Walkinshaw wrote. The next paragraph asked supporters to contribute to his reelection campaign.

Garcia’s campaign raised more than $700,000 in the third quarter of this year, bringing its total for the cycle to $3.3 million, according to Federal Election Commission data. The campaign ended September with $1.6 million on hand. Garcia’s seat is considered safely Democratic. He has also raised $1.4 million for the campaign arm of House Democrats this cycle, and over $1 million for the committee’s Red to Blue program that pushes resources to candidates trying to flip a Republican seat. The California Democrat also contributed $335,000 to fulfill his dues to the campaign arm.

A spokeswoman did not see an ethical issue, saying the solicitations provide clarity.

“Rep. Garcia is proud to be able to raise millions of dollars for the DCCC and candidates around the country,” Sara Guerrero, a spokesperson for Garcia, said in a statement. “He will continue to be straight up and clear to our supporters about what our agenda is and what will happen when we win the majority.”

entries.title: Tom Sietsema’s 5 Favorite Breakfasts in the D.C. Area
entries.summary: From can’t-miss breakfast tacos in Mt. Pleasant to stellar pancakes in Arlington, each of these restaurants makes for a great start to the day.
entries.content:
Like making your bed first thing in the morning, taking time for a sit-down breakfast is one of those gestures that instantly improves your day. No matter what lies ahead, you’ll come home to a straightened nest or go forth with fuel in your tank, respectively.

Breakfast is also the most democratic meal of the day, typically less expensive and performative than dinner, and a nice balance to the usual rush. I like to think of the morning meal as a satisfying act of resistance against a prepackaged protein bar at your desk or a container of yogurt knocked back in your car.

Those are among the lessons I learned as I spent the last month identifying some of the D.C. area’s best breakfasts away from home. As diverse as they are, each venue offers the bonus of a sense of community along with their menus — reason enough in my book to rise and shine.

La Tejana

Ana-Maria Jaramillo moved from Texas to D.C. for love eight years ago and promptly encountered heartbreak: Where were the breakfast tacos?

“I was very disappointed in the breakfast scene,” says Jaramillo, who missed her daily habit from back in McAllen, where she grew up, and Austin, where she went to college. Thus began a journey to fill the void, which started with Jaramillo peddling breakfast tacos from her stoop in Mt. Pleasant in 2019 and eventually opening a brick-and-mortar shop called Le Tejana four years later.

Along the way, she also perfected the vessel for her tacos. To visit the storefront these days is to chomp into a flour tortilla that relies on vegetable shortening and olive oil for moisture and manages to be simultaneously thin, malleable, fluffy and tasty, even without a filling.

The fillings are fab, though. The best-seller is 956, the area code for McAllen. Inside the bundle await refried beans, custardy scrambled eggs, fried potatoes, cilantro and bacon — a lot to like. Make mine a 512, the area code for Austin and meaty with another D.C. favorite: chopped brisket from 2Fifty Texas BBQ. Very good meatless breakfast tacos, one with tomatoes and poblano, are offered as well.

You can buy a single taco, but most requests are for three or six. Everything is homemade, sauces included. The tangy crowd-pleaser blends Greek yogurt, cilantro, lime juice and more.

Honestly, I adore everything about Le Tejana, save for the lines when I’m hangry. (The kitchen, headed up by Gus May, Jaramillo’s husband, turns out as many as 1,800 tacos on the weekend; a dedicated team of egg-crackers goes through an estimated 180 cases a week.) Rickety stairs lead to a spare, second-floor dining area dressed with blue tables and curtains for windows facing the street, a space available to rent for a gathering.

The name of the business and the faceless woman depicted on the packaging pay homage to the strong Latina women Jaramillo says inspired her back home. “It’s a symbol of what I want to represent,” says the entrepreneur, who gives away leftover tacos to her neighbors and has plans to expand. Without revealing too much, she teases that No. 2 will be in the District and open in “under a year.” I see more lines in her future.

3211 Mt. Pleasant St. NW
202-621-8509
latejanadc.com
Breakfast tacos $4.75 (for one) to $26 (for six)

The Market Lunch

If you want to know what distinguishes the eye openers at The Market Lunch inside Eastern Market from so many of its peers, just ask Tom Glasgow. “Everything we make is real,” says the owner of one of the most beloved institutions on Capitol Hill.

Sure enough, only fresh blueberries go into his signature, fluffy buckwheat pancakes, and never too soon to prevent the fruit from bursting on the griddle. Genuine maple syrup makes the best topper; coffee from Rise Up provides a potent chaser.

The crab cake platter with a choice of eggs shows off plenty of goodness, too. Eggs over easy are textbook definitions, and they’re served alongside potatoes that are boiled, chopped, deep-fried and tinted with (surprise!) Accent. The star of the plate, though, is the crab cake, shaped from jumbo lump crab from Cambridge, Md. Parsley, mayonnaise and mustard inform the mix, but mostly what you taste is local crab that’s brightened with a splash of fresh lemon juice at the end. A house-baked bun, crisped on the griddle, allows you to create your own breakfast sandwich.
Market_lunch.jpg (969x640, AR: 1.51)Another prize is the aptly-named “brick” that packs in a roll a choice of eggs, meat (go for the spicy sausage), fried potatoes and melted American cheese. Have extra napkins handy.

Customers join a line beneath a big chalkboard menu, give their order to a friendly face behind a counter, then wait for their names to be called. The process may take a few minutes; be patient. Sure, you can take your breakfast to go, but the better plan is to sit at Market Lunch’s long, worn, wood counter and soak up the scene as you eat. (The attraction unfolds in a Victorian building designed by Adolf Cluss, also responsible for the Smithsonian Arts and Industries Building.)

A sign on the wall, testament to the institution’s popularity, lays out some rules: “No saving seats” is one. “No reading of newspapers or laptops when we are crowded,” reads another.

Sound strict? It’s not. Glasgow, who’s watched over the place since 1978, turns out to be a softie who encourages tourists to try something they’re unfamiliar with (fried oysters, maybe) and shared that he shed a real tear the day the late civil rights activist and statesman John Lewis appeared in line.

“I enjoy what I do,” says the owner, 70, who adds that “the neatest people in the world” come through his place — and work there, I’d add.

225 7th St. SE (inside Eastern Market)
202-547-8444
marketlunchdc.com
Breakfast dishes $7.95 to $26.95

Parkway Deli & Restaurant

Breakfast for dinner is always an option at this popular Silver Spring storefront. So is dinner for breakfast. Which means one of you can be tackling eggs, pancakes and bacon during morning rush hour while another is slurping chicken soup, crammed with the obvious but also carrots, onions and egg noodles. Each spoonful goes down like a hug.

Launched in 1963, Parkway Deli, which opens with a food store, is in the hands of Danny Gurewitz, a third-generation owner. He reports an average of 300 diners visit each day. His recipe for success: “We have a large menu and people can pretty much get what they want.”

No problem if you want your bagel scooped out. The vibe is relaxed. A glance around the dining room — a sea of booths and bands of mirrors at eye level — finds lots of demographics, including kids sporting paper crowns and coloring with crayons provided by the restaurant.

For breakfast, I head for bronzed potato pancakes topped with eggs over easy and nova lox, or sometimes an omelet that’s a smidge smaller than an iPad, packed with green peppers, ham and melted cheese. Huge mugs of coffee make them feel bottomless.

Helping to keep the place busy are a popular pickle bar and a steady kitchen. Head chef Rene Santos has been a presence for 32 years. “He’ll never leave,” jokes his boss.

8317 Grubb Rd., Silver Spring
301-587-1427
theparkwaydeli.com
Breakfast dishes $10 to $18

Ruthie’s All-Day

Craving pancakes? You want the golden buttermilk saucers at this family-friendly dining room in Arlington Heights, where the order comes with a knob of butter that melts in the heat and a chunky apple compote lightly sweetened with maple syrup.

As much as the food, the sunny setting says “good morning,” thanks to green wainscoting, white subway tile, windows that look onto an umbrella-shaded patio, and an open kitchen. (Unlike at night, at breakfast you order at the counter, find your own seat, and pour your own water. Works for me!)

Ruthie’s list is just nine dishes long, but the treasures include one of the finest breakfast sandwiches in the area, scrambled eggs and herby pork sausage slipped between Ruthie’s craggy biscuits. Best to eat the construction with a knife and fork — and watch out for the warm rush of aioli. Prepare to cancel your lunch plans, too. Named for a long-ago food business at the same location, “Mr. W’s” biscuit amounts to a lot of fuel.

Speaking of generous, the $18 “big plate” brings together a palooza of two eggs, house-made bacon, beef sausage, chive-flecked hash browns and biscuits baked on site. Small wonder two diners often opt to split the largesse. That’s never an issue with the restaurant, which in the a.m. fills with parents (some with babies in tow), Pentagon types and the occasional critic in search of a meal deal. (Ruthie’s is where I sometimes direct mourners after services at Arlington National Cemetery, less than 10 minutes away.)

Good news for Fairfax: A spinoff, from chef Matt Hill and general manager Todd Salvadore, opened in April, giving locals fresh reason to rise and shine and the owners a chance to “make some new friends,” says Salvadore.

3411 5th St South, Arlington
703-888-2841
ruthiesallday.com
Breakfast dishes $8 to $18

Seasons

Here’s where bold-face names and power brokers like to start their day, and not just because the tables in the light-filled, carpet-softened dining room in the Four Seasons hotel are surrounded by pools of space. (One strains to eavesdrop, in other words.) There’s the warm reception at the host stand, a spread of newspapers for those who want their information from dead trees, and such niceties on the broad tables as fresh flowers and those tiny jars of marmalade that may or may not end up in a purse or pocket by meal’s end. I couldn’t help but smile when I looked up to see light fixtures framed in sunbursts.

Water and coffee come quickly – welcome touches when you might be getting billed by the hour by a tablemate.

Seasons’ menu checks all the breakfast boxes. What I appreciate is the unexpected ground the list also covers. A Turkish-inspired plate found a poached egg atop eggplant-tomato confit in a ring of sesame-seeded simit bread — an artful and delicious combination that transports you to Istanbul in every bite. When two of us were debating dishes, our attendant volunteered to split them both on our respective plates. And so it was that we both got tastes of finely minced corned beef hash and chorizo molletes (an open-faced Mexican sandwich with refried beans and Oaxacan cheese).

Watching your diet? Seek out the keto plate, bulked up with grilled halloumi, wagyu beef and sauerkraut, among other accompaniments. The purple-colored smoothie powered with berries, yogurt, soy milk and oat bran helps out, too.

As befits the Four Seasons, the service and extra touches are tops. Expect an elegant biscotti on your coffee saucer and a skewer of blueberries garnishing your smoothie. When I ordered a fruit plate in addition to another breakfast dish, my server talked me down to a half-portion, which was still generous for a solo diner. No fewer than eight different fruits arrived, beautifully arranged in their bowl. Leftovers were packed in a bag that included compostable utensils. “A sword for your hash,” said a server who set down a big carved knife for the corned beef hash. Seasons has a sense of humor to boot.

2800 Pennsylvania Ave. NW
202-342-0444
fourseasons.com
Breakfast entrees $24 to $72
